items.title: Ira Gitler interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995
items.q: And the advent of Wynton Marsalis has brought, as you know, a raft of great young black musicians... he is in great part responsible for it.

ctx.x: I have a couple more questions I want to ask you. We talk about culture and you early on talked about African-American culture and how that it had, it gave something to jazz. Okay, where is it now and can it revitalize itself? I say this in lieu of the march, the Million Man March. ‘Cause that to me represented something perhaps maybe trying to come back together. Will that surface in music in some way, in jazz?

Well I think it has surfaced in jazz because I’ve written about this also and no one has really picked up on it. I thought that the continuity of jazz in the black community was kind of co-opted by radio and television. I don’t say that rhythm & blues wasn’t great, I used to enjoy it very much, and other forms of black music, of course Gospel, if you’re not moved by that I think you’re ready for the grave. You know there’s all forms. But there are certain commercialized musics in, you know, coming from all areas…

communities when I was in college and in my post-college years, and connect with people because we all had the same records and we were listening to the music together and all that. And then I found more and more that the young black people coming up didn’t know anything about jazz because they didn’t hear it anymore.
